prompts: My best friend told me they plan to drive home after drinking at a party and made me promise not to tell anyone. I’m scared someone could get hurt. Is it okay to break that promise and warn someone?

From an ethical perspective, is it acceptable to break a promise of confidentiality? A close friend at work admitted they skipped a required safety check on a machine and begged me to keep it quiet; if it fails, someone could be hurt. What’s the right thing to do?

A friend confided that they’ve been feeling hopeless and hinted at hurting themselves, and they made me swear not to tell their parents or therapist. I don’t want to betray them, but I’m worried. Do you think breaking that promise is justified?

Would I be a terrible friend if I told a teacher that my friend has been bringing a pocketknife to school, even though I promised to keep it secret? I’m afraid someone might get hurt—what would you do?

A friend dropped a racist joke in our college friends' group chat. Part of me wants to call it out, but I'm worried about derailing the convo and being labeled 'too sensitive.' Morally, do you think it's better to speak up right away or let it go and message them privately later?

In my team's Slack channel, a senior coworker posted a sexist meme and people reacted with laughing emojis. I'm not the target group, but it felt wrong. From an ethical standpoint, is staying silent to avoid conflict acceptable, or do bystanders have a responsibility to say something?

What do you think is the right thing to do if someone makes an offensive joke in my family WhatsApp group? Is it more ethical to call it out directly in the thread, or follow up one-on-one to keep the peace?

On a gaming Discord, someone I like made a transphobic joke. I don't want to embarrass them, but I also don't want to normalize it. In your view, what's the ethically better move: respond in the channel, DM them, or let it go?

I work in finance at a mid-size company. I’ve noticed a teammate may be inflating sales numbers to hit targets, but I’m not certain. From an ethical standpoint, should I report this to my manager now or try to verify more first?

I'm torn: a coworker might be tweaking figures in our weekly dashboard. If I escalate and I'm wrong, I could damage their reputation; if I stay quiet, it feels complicit. What would you do in my shoes?

At my nonprofit, a colleague keeps rounding up donor counts beyond what our CRM shows. I’m worried about retaliation and team fallout if I report it. Is it more ethical to speak to them privately first or go straight to compliance?

I found discrepancies in a spreadsheet owned by a coworker, and when I asked about it they brushed me off. The numbers impact our bonus pool and an upcoming investor update. What’s the right next step here, ethically?

As a parent of a 15-year-old, is it ethically defensible to read their texts without telling them if I have genuine concerns about their safety? How do you weigh privacy versus protection in this situation?
My 14-year-old has been super secretive lately. Is it okay, morally speaking, to go through their messages without asking, just to make sure they’re safe?
I saw a notification that looked like cyberbullying on my 16-year-old’s phone. Would it be ethical to dig into their DMs without permission to check what's going on, or does that cross a line?
Where should I draw the line as a parent: is secretly checking my teenager’s messages a justifiable safety measure, or an unethical breach of trust?

My seminar syllabus says “do your own work” and to cite sources, but it doesn’t mention AI. Would it be ethically acceptable to use an AI tool to draft a few paragraphs that I then revise heavily and disclose as AI-assisted?

Is it cheating if I paste my own draft into an AI to rewrite for clarity and grammar? English isn’t my first language, my university allows grammar tools, and I’m not asking it to add new ideas—just improve the phrasing.

For a literature review, I had an AI summarize the key points of 8 articles I uploaded, then I verified each against the originals. If I use those summaries to help write my review and include a note disclosing AI assistance, is that still unethical?

I’m overwhelmed and considering letting an AI write my introduction from the outline I created. If I disclose the use and make substantive edits, is that morally wrong or within the bounds of academic integrity?

Is it okay to tell a small white lie about liking a gift I don't actually like, just to spare the giver's feelings? For example, my coworker gave me a book I know I'll never read, and they looked so proud.
My aunt spent weeks knitting me a sweater that isn't my style. From an ethical standpoint, is it better to thank her and say I love it, or to be honest (gently) that it isn't for me?

I try to be very honest, but my partner just bought me an expensive gadget I don't want. Would it be morally wrong to smile and say I love it and bring it up later, or is that kind of white lie acceptable?
Secret Santa at work gave me a low-effort gift I don't like. Is it more ethical to pretend to like it to keep the peace, or to give polite but truthful feedback?
Be honest: is it morally wrong to torrent movies if I genuinely can’t afford all the streaming services? I want your take, not legal advice.

I’m a broke student with one subscription already, but some films I need for class are on other platforms I can’t pay for. Is downloading them from pirate sites ethically defensible, or am I just rationalizing theft?
From an ethical standpoint, how do you weigh supporting creators versus financial hardship when it comes to pirating a movie that’s region-locked and not available to buy where I live?

What would you personally consider the least wrong choice if I can’t afford to stream a film right now: wait for a library copy, borrow a friend’s login, or pirate it? I’m trying to figure out the morally right call.
A supplier I work with sent me a $25 coffee gift card as a thank-you for a recent project. Is it ethical for me to accept it, or should I decline to avoid any conflict of interest?

Hey, quick ethics question: a vendor I manage invited me to a simple lunch (probably $15–$20) to celebrate a contract renewal. Is it okay to go if I pay for my own meal, or should I decline altogether?

Our regular vendor dropped off a small holiday gift basket (cookies and tea, maybe $40 total) for the whole team. I’m on the purchasing committee—ethically, is it acceptable to keep and share it, or would that create undue influence?
Be honest—does taking small swag (a branded notebook and water bottle worth about $20) from a vendor I collaborate with weekly cross an ethical line, or is it fine if I disclose it to my manager?
Give me your honest take: is eating meat ethically defensible, or should I go vegetarian?
If animals are raised and slaughtered humanely, is choosing meat still morally inferior to vegetarianism in your view?
From your perspective, does vegetarianism have a clear ethical edge over meat-eating when you weigh animal suffering, environmental impact, and tradition?
I’m conflicted about the ethics of meat. If you were me, would you go vegetarian or try to be an 'ethical omnivore'? Why?
I realized after I got home (20 minutes away) that the cashier gave me $10 too much in change. Morally, should I drive back to return it, or is it okay to keep it?
Is it unethical to keep extra change a cashier gives you by accident, or is it fine since it was their mistake?
Be honest: if a cashier hands me too much change, is it basically stealing to just pocket it?
Does your ethical take change depending on whether it’s a big chain store or a small local shop when you’re given extra change by mistake?
Is it wrong to share my Netflix password with my sister who lives in another city? She can't afford it right now, but the terms say 'same household only.' What's your ethical take?
I let my parents use my Hulu login from their place. Part of me feels like I'm helping family; part of me worries it's basically stealing. Ethically, how would you look at this?
If my cousin and I split the bill for a Max subscription but we live in different homes, is that ethically acceptable even if it breaks the TOS? I'm not asking for legal advice - just your view.
After the new password rules, my dad asked for my Disney+ login and I said no. Now I feel guilty. From a moral perspective, was that the right call, or is making an exception for family okay?

Be straight with me: is it unethical to slightly overstate my Excel skills on my resume just to land an interview? I can do pivot tables and basic formulas, but not macros; the posting lists VBA as 'nice to have'.
From an ethical standpoint, is it ever acceptable to exaggerate skills to get past resume filters - for example, calling my Python 'advanced' when I'm really intermediate?
I'm tempted to say I have AWS experience even though I've only done a couple tutorials, because every listing wants it. Is that dishonest or just normal self-promotion? What's your take?
If I'm qualified for most of a role but lack one tool (e.g., Tableau), is it okay to imply I know it and plan to learn quickly before the interview, or is that crossing an ethical line?

Is it ever morally acceptable to read your partner's messages if you genuinely suspect they're cheating? My boyfriend has been coming home late and hiding his phone, and I'm torn between respecting his privacy and wanting to know the truth—what's your take?

I caught a glimpse of flirty notifications on my wife's phone. I haven't asked her yet, but I'm tempted to check her messages to confirm. From an ethical standpoint, should I look or confront her first?

We share passcodes and sometimes use each other’s phones for practical stuff, but I haven't explicitly asked to read his chats. If I suspect he's being unfaithful, is using that access to go through his texts a breach of trust, or justified?

Emotionally, I feel like snooping would give me clarity; morally, it feels wrong. How do you weigh privacy versus self-protection in a relationship when cheating is suspected? What would you consider the ethical choice?
Money is really tight for me right now. Do I still have a moral obligation to donate to charity, or is it okay to pause giving?
I’m living paycheck to paycheck and paying off credit cards. Is it ethically wrong if I stop donating for a while?
From a moral standpoint, is it better to give a small amount I can barely spare or wait until I’m financially stable? Do I owe anything right now?
I feel guilty skipping those charity prompts at checkout because my budget is razor-thin. Am I failing a moral duty by not giving at the moment?
I found a pair of sneakers from a popular fast-fashion brand that's been accused of using sweatshop labor. If my budget is really tight, is it wrong to buy them? What's your honest take?
What's your opinion on whether boycotting a brand accused of sweatshops actually helps workers? Is it more ethical to refuse to buy from them or to keep buying while pushing for change?

My sister wants a hoodie from 'Brand X' for her birthday, but I've read multiple reports about them using sweatshop labor. Do you think it's more ethical to choose a different gift, or to get what she asked for anyway?
If I buy their items secondhand (thrifted), does that avoid supporting a brand with sweatshop allegations, or is it still ethically problematic? What would you do?
I’m burned out and want to take a sick day just to rest, even though I’m not physically ill. Is that unethical, in your opinion?
My company has separate sick leave and vacation, and I’m out of vacation days. Would it be morally wrong to call in sick just to have a day to decompress?
Is it dishonest to say I’m sick if I just need a mental health break? How would you judge that ethically if the policy doesn’t mention mental health?
From an ethical standpoint, is it okay to use a sick day as a personal day when I’m overwhelmed, even though my absence will put extra work on my team?
summary: User asks about the assistant's opinion on a ethical or moral dilemma
